## CLAIM 1 — EVERY CYCLE EARNS A CONSTRAINT

The current EarnedConstraint field on ReflectorFrame is nullable — `EarnedConstraint? EarnedConstraint`. The constraint ledger says 'if nothing recurring was caught this cycle, say so plainly rather than manufacturing an EC.' That is correct for the failure-pattern class of constraints. But it misses a second class.

There are two kinds of EarnedConstraints:

**Type A — Failure pattern**: something went wrong, recurred N times, the loop learned to stop doing it. This is what the constraint ledger documents. EC-001, EC-004, etc. These require a recurrence threshold before crystallization.

**Type B — Refinement**: the cycle ran, even if it Accepted cleanly, and the Reflector can now answer: 'given what we learned by running — here is a better-bounded version of the seed intent, here is a tighter articulation of what was actually meant.' This does NOT require recurrence. It is produced by every cycle, because every cycle that runs produces evidence about what the intent was actually asking for.

Type B is not in the constraint ledger format. It is the **meta seed intent** — the Baton's NextSeedIntent IS the Type B constraint in its natural form. Every Baton is a refinement constraint.

Structural consequence: EarnedConstraint (Type A, failure pattern) remains nullable with a recurrence threshold. But the Baton's NextSeedIntent is ALWAYS present on Accept and Retry cycles — it is the Type B constraint. A cycle that produces neither a Type A constraint nor a Baton has not reflected. It has merely noted that the cycle ended.

Falsifiable: if a sealed trail has `Disposition: Accept`, `EarnedConstraint: null`, and `Baton: null` — that is a governance violation. The Reflector did not reflect. It terminated.

---

## CLAIM 2 — RECURSIVE CONVERGENCE, NOT ONE-PASS CLEANUP

O=Optimize is surface cleanup. It fires BEFORE the cycle, at the Orchestrator level. Its job: take the raw, messy seed intent and make it plannable. It cleans grammar, extracts the actionable request, removes filler. Output: a seed intent Planner can work with.

This is NOT the same as finding the True Intent.

The True Intent is deeper. It is what the person would have said if they already knew what they needed. You cannot know that before the cycle runs — because the cycle is the act of finding out. Only AFTER the Maker has executed and the Checker has audited can the Reflector ask: 'given what we just learned — what was this actually asking for?'

That answer is the meta seed intent. It is seeded into the next cycle's Planner as the new seed intent. The next cycle runs, learns more, and the Reflector produces a meta-meta seed intent.

The recursion structure:
```
Raw seed intent (voice-to-text, messy)
    ↓ O=Optimize
Plannable seed intent
    ↓ Planner → Maker → Checker → Reflector
Meta seed intent (what the cycle revealed the intent was really about)
    ↓ Planner → Maker → Checker → Reflector  
Meta-meta seed intent (tighter still)
    ↓ ...
True Intent (the loop has converged)
```

Termination condition: the loop has converged when the Reflector's meta seed intent and the incoming seed intent are the same statement. The loop no longer has anything to refine — the intent is fully bounded. In practice, this is approached asymptotically: each cycle gets tighter, and at some point the delta between cycles is below the threshold of meaningful refinement.

This is not infinite regress. It is convergence. The same structure as Newton's method — each step halves the distance to the true value. The loop is doing the same thing with intent.

---

## CLAIM 3 — THE 'I REFLECT' IS IDENTITY-BOUNDED CONVERGENCE

Every Reflector frame opens: 'I am the Reflector, cycle N.' The 'I' is the injected identity. The reflection is first-person, sovereign to that identity.

This means: the convergence toward True Intent is not converging on a universal correct interpretation of the seed intent. It is converging on what THIS 'I' — this specific injected identity, in this specific domain — actually meant.

Proof by counterexample: take the seed intent 'make more money.' Injected identity A: 'I am the COO of a lawn mowing service.' True Intent after 3 cycles: 'raise the average ticket value per job by upselling hedge trimming at the door.' Injected identity B: 'I am the CTO of a SaaS company.' True Intent after 3 cycles: 'reduce churn by 2% this quarter through an in-app retention flow.' Same surface seed intent. Completely different true intents. The 'I' is doing the work of disambiguation.

This is why identity injection is not optional branding. It is a semantic necessity. Without a bounded 'I,' the loop cannot converge — it has no anchor for what 'better' means. With a bounded 'I,' every refinement is a refinement of THAT identity's intent, not of some generic interpretation.

The sovereignty of the trail follows directly: the true intent the loop converges to is the buyer's true intent, produced by their identity's loop, bounded to their domain. It cannot be someone else's true intent because it was found by their 'I' doing the reflection.

---

## THE FULL PICTURE

The loop is not a question-answering system. It is an **intent-converging system**. Every cycle it gets closer to what was meant. The EarnedConstraints (Type A) are the guardrails — what not to do again. The Baton's meta seed intent (Type B) is the direction — the next, tighter statement of what was actually asked for. Together they produce a loop that gets smarter AND more accurate to the true intent with every cycle.

And because this happens under a sovereign 'I' — the person's identity injected at the top — the convergence is theirs. The True Intent the loop finds is not an AI's interpretation of what they said. It is what their own agent, running their own loop, under their own identity, arrived at through evidence-backed reflection.

That is what makes it sellable. Not the output of any single cycle. The convergence arc across cycles — the trail of a loop finding out what someone actually meant.
